title: US to blacklist Asian AI firm Megaspeed
content:
US to blacklist Asian AI firm Megaspeed after Nvidia scandal
- Published
The US has said it intends to ban a Singaporean artificial intelligence (AI) company allegedly tied to the Nvidia scandal from doing business in America.
The Department of Commerce announced it planned to add Megaspeed Ltd to a list of entities that are blacklisted from buying or selling goods in the US.
The company is mainly a developer of data centres, but in recent weeks a former executive of Megaspeed was accused of working as spy for China while having a romantic relationship with Nvidia head Jensen Huang.
The relationship led to additional scrutiny by US officials and heightened concern that Megaspeed was funnelling Nvidia's advanced AI computer chips to China.
When exactly the ban against Megaspeed will go into effect was not specified in the commerce department announcement. The BBC has asked the agency for comment, along with the White House and Megaspeed.
Megaspeed was not well known within the US until last month when media reports emerged that a former Megaspeed executive, Alice Huang, had an affair with Jensen Huang.
Alice Huang (no relation) was thought by US intelligence to be working as an asset for Beijing, creating national security concerns within the US.
China has denied that she is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" on AI technology.
On 12 November, Jensen Huang resigned after allegations he had had another affair, this one with a Nvidia employee.
On Monday, Nvidia's board reinstated him after US President Donald Trump said he had "convinced" the company and "made the deal".
The commerce department has said it had been investigating Megaspeed for almost two years.
The department said it had suspected the company was violating US export controls by helping to get Nvidia's chips into the hands of companies within China.
China has been blocked from buying such technology since 2022.
Although based in Singapore, Megaspeed has significant business dealings in China.
Alibaba, for instance, the major Chinese online retailer, has been reported to be one if its largest customers.
Megaspeed was a known buyer of billions of dollars of Nvidia computer chips, including through its subsidiary Speedmatrix, which has also been added to the Commerce blacklist.
Nvidia's computer chips, originally designed for use in gaming consols, in recent years have become crucial to the continued growth of the AI industry.
Without enough supply or access to computer chips that are capable of processing the huge amount of data needed to make things like AI chatbots and models run, AI companies will not be able to meet or grow demand from people using AI tools.
That has driven up the value of Nvidia on the stock market, as well as its influence in the AI industry and the White House.
Although tech stocks have in recent months been volatile and trending lower, when Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia because of his affairs, the company's stock fell by more than 30%.
Anxiety about the company's influence and ability to operate within the AI ecosystem without its famed executive appeared to take down shares of other tech companies, too.
Huang was reinstated on Monday to his position as head of Nvidia, a move that US President Donald Trump said he told the company's board to take.
The company's stock rallied on his reinstatement, as did several other tech stocks, but shares of Nvidia did not climb to where the company had been before being immersed in scandal.
In the weeks ahead, Huang and the company he now runs again are facing multiple government agency investigations.
Huang and the chief legal officer of Nvidia are set to appear next for a closed-door briefing with the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

report.summary: US moves to blacklist Singapore-based Megaspeed and subsidiary Speedmatrix over alleged diversion of Nvidia AI chips to China, amid a spy scandal involving Nvidia's CEO.
report.background: The action follows nearly two years of US Commerce Department scrutiny into whether Megaspeed, a Singapore data-centre developer with substantial China business, helped move advanced Nvidia AI chips into China despite US export controls imposed in 2022. Nvidia's GPUs became the scarce backbone of generative AI, giving the company outsized market and political influence. Singapore has served as a regional trading and data-centre hub, but US officials worry it can also be a transshipment point. The case intensified after reports that former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, no relation to Jensen Huang, had a relationship with Nvidia's CEO and was suspected by US intelligence of working for Beijing; China denied the spy allegation. Nvidia's CEO resigned in November after separate affair allegations and was reinstated by the board after President Trump intervened. The Commerce Department also added Megaspeed subsidiary Speedmatrix to the proposed blacklist.
key_points: The US Commerce Department plans to add Megaspeed and its subsidiary Speedmatrix to its entity list, which would bar them from buying or selling US goods and technology. The announcement did not specify when the ban would take effect, and agencies have not commented publicly on the timing.

Officials suspect Megaspeed violated US export controls by helping Nvidia chips reach Chinese companies. The Singapore-based firm had significant China dealings and was a known buyer of billions of dollars of Nvidia chips; Alibaba has been reported as one of its largest customers.

The case exploded into a spy scandal after reports that former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang had a romantic relationship with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and was suspected by US intelligence of being a Beijing asset. China denied she is a spy and warned against using the affair as a pretext for a technology blockade.

Nvidia's CEO resigned on 12 November after separate affair allegations and was reinstated by the board after President Trump intervened. Nvidia stock fell more than 30% on his resignation, rallied on his return, but remained below pre-scandal levels, while other tech stocks also moved on the news.

The blacklist adds to wider US-China tensions over AI compute. Washington has blocked China from buying advanced chips since 2022, and the Megaspeed case signals closer scrutiny of Singapore and other intermediaries that may be used to route restricted Nvidia hardware into China.
report.impact: The proposed blacklist raises compliance risk across the AI supply chain. If finalized, Megaspeed and Speedmatrix would be cut off from US chips and software, potentially disrupting data-centre capacity and cloud access in Asia and making Nvidia GPU flows more tightly scrutinized. For the AI industry, it reinforces that export controls are becoming a core competitive variable: access to advanced compute, not just algorithms, determines who can train and serve models at scale. Developers may see tighter cloud-provider screening, regional availability limits and higher costs for GPU capacity, especially in Singapore and China-linked projects. Regular users could feel this through slower rollouts, higher prices or reduced access to some AI services. Nvidia's leadership turmoil and continuing investigations add uncertainty for partners and investors, even as demand for AI chips remains strong.
report.tools: Readers tracking this should watch the US Bureau of Industry and Security's Entity List and Consolidated Screening List, plus open-source sanctions screening via OpenSanctions. For technical context on compute constraints, follow Nvidia's GPU and export-compliance disclosures and open-source inference stacks such as vLLM, Hugging Face Transformers and PyTorch, which show how efficiently limited GPU capacity can be used. Cloud providers' regional GPU availability pages are also useful.
